status: Seven preserved v2 visual examples; revised v3 text/schema evaluated independently. Exact targets excluded as before.

examples.guidance: Hooman explicitly rates this printer scene FAIL. Although it has a dedicated support and pleasant décor, the rigid printer edges do not align with the table edges. Compare the front and side axes carefully: do not dismiss this visible mismatch as a stylish angle or award a pass merely because the support looks usable. The surrounding furniture must also form a coherent aligned arrangement. This illustrates the required sensitivity to device/table alignment.

Hooman explicitly rates this printer scene FAIL. He expects a wall-aligned printer set back toward the wall and toward a practical side of the table; this conspicuous isolated placement wastes the surface and looks staged rather than naturally arranged. Being on a table separate from the meeting desk is insufficient. Judge the position and body axes relative to the entire wall-backed table, not just lack of obstacles.

Hooman explicitly rates this laptop scene FAIL. The laptop is too far into the broad tabletop and away from an actual user chair. The surrounding work objects do not make a coherent reachable laptop station. A laptop must sit near the person using it with an unobstructed keyboard work area. Do not excuse this as a shared table or an attractive conference scene.

Hooman explicitly rates this laptop scene FAIL. The visible chair is in front of the notebook area while the laptop is too far away to the left/back for natural seated typing. He likes the scene narrative, but that appeal cannot rescue failed reach and chair alignment. Assess depth and sideways displacement from the actual chair, not a hypothetical chair placed at the keyboard.

C-Tech flags: "v13 product is floating". Inspect how the laptop base plane sits relative to the table plane: a low corner and some shadow are not sufficient evidence that the entire load-bearing base is convincingly supported. This is a contact_integration defect (floating), not simply a styling preference.

Reference photograph: a printer on its own cabinet, operating front facing the standing user and an open paper-output path. This illustrates natural printer access without a chair. It is an explanatory support/access example, not a human-labeled perfect overall score.

Reference photograph: the printer is on a separate table in the background while laptop activity uses the foreground table. A neighboring workspace is compatible with natural printer placement when its support and approach are separate. Some printer details are too distant to score confidently.
